Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$, let $q\in R^{\times}$, let $d,n\ge0$
with $d\ge n$, and let $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Write
$S:=S(d,n)=\mathrm{End}_H(M)$ for the type-A q-Schur algebra with
$M=\bigoplus_{\mu\in\Lambda(d,n)}M^{\mu}$ the direct sum of the permutation
modules ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]],
[[def-direct-sum-of-a-family-of-modules]]) and let
$\{\varphi_{ST}:\lambda\in\Lambda^{+}(d,n),\ S,T\in T_0(\lambda)\}$ be its
cellular semistandard basis ([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]]
for the underlying Murphy elements and
[[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]] for the standard
basis along which this basis is defined). Put
$\omega:=(1^n)\in\Lambda(d,n)$, the composition with $n$ parts equal to $1$
(legitimate because $d\ge n$), so that the Young subgroup $S_\omega$ is trivial
and $m_\omega=1$; hence
$$M^{\omega}=m_\omega H=H$$
is the regular right $H$-module. Let $t^{\omega}$ be the unique standard
$\omega$-tableau, with entries $1,2,\dots,n$ down its single column; it is in
particular the unique row-standard $\omega$-tableau whose entries increase down
the column. Set
$$e:=\varphi_{t^{\omega}t^{\omega}}\in S.$$

Then:

1. $e$ is the projection of $M$ onto the direct summand $M^{\omega}=H$ along
   the other summands $M^{\mu}$, $\mu\ne\omega$; in particular $e^2=e$ and
   $$eSe\cong\mathrm{End}_H(M^{\omega})=\mathrm{End}_H(H),$$ via the algebra
   isomorphism
   $$\rho:H\longrightarrow eSe,\qquad h\longmapsto\rho_h,\qquad \rho_h(x):=hx,$$
   left multiplication by $h$ on $M^{\omega}=H$ being a right $H$-module
   endomorphism. Here the isomorphism $eSe\cong\mathrm{End}_H(M^{\omega})$
   sends $efe$ to $f|_{M^{\omega}}$ and is inverted by extending an
   endomorphism of $M^{\omega}$ by zero on the other summands, and the
   identification $\mathrm{End}_H(H)\cong H$ sends an endomorphism to its value
   at $1$. By the construction of the semistandard basis elements $\varphi_{ST}$
   (Mathas (4.13) with Corollaries 4.9 and 4.12; see the locator above), the
   diagonal element $\varphi_{t^{\omega}t^{\omega}}$ is exactly the
   endomorphism of $M$ that is the identity on $M^{\omega}$ and zero on all
   $M^{\mu}$ with $\mu\ne\omega$, which is the projection asserted above.
2. The **Schur functor** is
   $$F:\mathrm{mod}\text{-}S\longrightarrow\mathrm{mod}\text{-}H,\qquad F(X):=Xe=X\otimes_SSe,$$
   with the right $H$-action transported along $\rho$, so that
   $(xe)\cdot h:=x\,\rho_h$ for $x\in X$, $h\in H$
   ([[def-left-and-right-modules]]). It is exact and $R$-linear on morphisms:
   since $e^2=e$, the right $S$-module $Se$ is a direct summand of the regular
   right $S$-module $S$, so $X\mapsto X\otimes_SSe$ is a direct summand of the
   identity functor $X\mapsto X\otimes_SS\cong X$, which is exact; equivalently,
   right multiplication by $e$ is a direct-summand projection on underlying
   $R$-modules and the functor is a composition of the exact functors
   $X\mapsto X\otimes_SS$ and the idempotent projection $X\mapsto Xe$. The
   convention is fixed: the functor is $X\mapsto Xe$ on the right, and the
   left-module formula $X\mapsto eX$ is not used on this page.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^{\times}$, $d,n\ge0$, and
$H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ ([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Let $\Lambda(d,n)$ be
the set of compositions $\mu=(\mu_1,\dots,\mu_d)$ of $n$ (so $\mu_i\in\mathbb N$
and $\sum_i\mu_i=n$). For $\mu\in\Lambda(d,n)$ let
$m_\mu=\sum_{w\in S_\mu}T_w$
([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]]) and let $M^{\mu}:=m_\mu H$
be the right ideal it generates, the **(Hecke) permutation module**; $M^{\mu}$
is free over $R$ with basis
$\{m_\mu T_{d(t)}:t\text{ row-standard }\mu\text{-tableau}\}$ and is the Hecke
analogue of the module induced from the trivial representation of the Young
subgroup ([[def-young-subgroup-tabloid-and-permutation-module]]).

Here is the freeness statement in detail: the cosets $S_\mu d$ with $d\in D_\mu$
partition $S_n$, and $\ell(ud)=\ell(u)+\ell(d)$ for $u\in S_\mu$, $d\in D_\mu$
([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]]), so the standard basis
theorem ([[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]) gives
$T_uT_{d(t)}=T_{ud(t)}$ and
$m_\mu T_{d(t)}=\sum_{u\in S_\mu}T_{u\,d(t)}$; these are the standard basis
elements indexed by the single coset $S_\mu d(t)$, and the cosets are disjoint,
whence $M^\mu=\bigoplus_tR\,m_\mu T_{d(t)}$ is free with the displayed basis as
$t$ runs over the row-standard $\mu$-tableaux.

Put $M:=\bigoplus_{\mu\in\Lambda(d,n)}M^{\mu}$
([[def-direct-sum-of-a-family-of-modules]]) and define the **q-Schur algebra**
$$S(d,n):=\mathrm{End}_H(M),$$
the $R$-algebra of right $H$-module endomorphisms of $M$
([[def-left-and-right-modules]]).

**Cellular structure.** For all $\mu,\nu\in\Lambda(d,n)$,
$\mathrm{Hom}_H(M^{\mu},M^{\nu})$ is free with a basis indexed by row-semistandard
tableaux; for every partition $\lambda$ of $n$ with at most $d$ parts and all
semistandard $\lambda$-tableaux $S,T$ there is an element
$\varphi_{ST}\in S(d,n)$
([[def-semistandard-tableau-and-kostka-number]]), and the family
$$\{\varphi_{ST}:\lambda\in\Lambda^{+}(d,n),\ S,T\in T_0(\lambda)\},$$
where $\Lambda^{+}(d,n)$ is the set of partitions of $n$ with at most $d$ parts
ordered by dominance $\unrhd$ ([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]]), is an
$R$-basis of $S(d,n)$; the map $\varphi_{ST}\mapsto\varphi_{TS}$ is an algebra
anti-automorphism and the triangular axiom holds modulo the span of the
$\varphi_{UV}$ with $\mu\rhd\lambda$. Hence
$(\varphi,\Lambda^{+}(d,n))$ is a dominance-cellular basis of $S(d,n)$
([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]) and its cell modules are the
**Weyl modules** $W^{\lambda}$, free over $R$ with basis
$\{\varphi_T:T\in T_0(\lambda)\}$. Over a field $F$, $W^{\lambda}$ has nonzero
simple head $L^{\lambda}$, the $L^{\lambda}$ for
$\lambda\in\Lambda^{+}(d,n)$ form a complete set of pairwise non-isomorphic
absolutely irreducible $S(d,n)$-modules, and the decomposition matrix satisfies
$d_{\lambda\lambda}=1$ and $d_{\lambda\mu}\ne0\Rightarrow\lambda\unrhd\mu$.

**Semistandard idempotents and weight spaces.** In the same semistandard basis
the diagonal elements are orthogonal idempotents: $\varphi_{TT}^2=\varphi_{TT}$
and $\varphi_{SS}\varphi_{TT}=0$ for $S\ne T$ (Mathas Theorem 4.14, R. Green's
Semistandard Basis Theorem, printed p. 42; equivalently Dipper-James-Mathas,
The (Q,q)-Schur algebra, Section 5, where the diagonal semistandard elements
form a set of orthogonal idempotents whose sum is the identity of the Schur
algebra). For each composition $\nu\in\Lambda(d,n)$ let $T^{\nu}$ be the
row-semistandard $\nu$-tableau with all entries in row $i$ equal to $i$, so
that $T^{\nu}$ has shape $\nu$ and type $\nu$; the element
$\varphi_{T^{\nu}T^{\nu}}$ is the projection onto the $\nu$-weight space.
Over a field $F$ the weight-space dimensions of the Weyl modules are the Kostka
numbers:
$$\dim_F\bigl(W^{\lambda}\varphi_{T^{\nu}T^{\nu}}\bigr)=K_{\lambda\nu}=|T_0(\lambda,\nu)|$$
for $\lambda\in\Lambda^{+}(d,n)$ and $\nu\in\Lambda(d,n)$ (Mathas Lemma 5.30
with Theorem 4.16, printed pp. 55-60; [[def-semistandard-tableau-and-kostka-number]]).

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $q\in R^{\times}$. With the Murphy cellular
basis $(\mathcal M,\Lambda)$ of $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$
([[thm-murphy-tableau-elements-form-a-cellular-basis]],
[[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]) and the canonical tableau
$t^\lambda$ of shape $\lambda\vdash n$
([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]]), the **Murphy cell
module** $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ is the right cell module $C^{\lambda}$ of the
Murphy basis: it is the free $R$-module with basis
$\{m_t:=m_{t^\lambda t}:t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)\}$ - the classes of the
Murphy elements whose *first* index is the canonical tableau - and $H$ acts by
$m_th=\sum_vr_vm_v$ whenever
$m_{t^\lambda t}h\equiv\sum_vr_vm_{t^\lambda v}\pmod{H^{\rhd\lambda}}$. (The
cellular action rule transforms the second index and fixes the first, so the
diagonal elements $m_{tt}$ alone do not span a submodule; the module basis is
the fixed-first-index family above.) Its **cell form** is the unique bilinear
form $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_\lambda:S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}\times
S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}\to R$ with
$$m_{us}m_{tv}\equiv\langle m_s,m_t\rangle_\lambda\,m_{uv}\pmod{H^{\rhd\lambda}}$$
for all $s,t,u,v\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)$; it is symmetric and associative and
$\mathrm{rad}\,S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ is a submodule, so
$D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}:=S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}/\mathrm{rad}\,S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$
is a right $H$-module
([[lem-cell-form-is-associative-and-its-radical-is-a-submodule]]).

**Convention (Dipper-James signed cellular normalization).** Let $\theta:H\to H$
be the involutive algebra automorphism defined by
$\theta(T_i)=-qT_i^{-1}=(q-1)-T_i$
([[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]]). For a right module $M$,
write $M^\theta$ for the same $R$-module with action $x\cdot h=x\theta(h)$. The
page's ordinary Specht normalization is the signed conjugate Murphy
construction
$$S^{\lambda}:=(S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta,$$
where $\lambda'$ is the conjugate partition ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). Its form is the form of
$S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}$ on the same underlying module; because $\theta$
commutes with $*$ this is associative for the twisted action
([[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]]). Over a field put
$$D^{\lambda}:=S^{\lambda}/\operatorname{rad}_{\rm form}S^{\lambda}=(D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta.$$
Thus $S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}=(S^{\lambda})^\theta$ and
$D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}=(D^{\lambda})^\theta$; conjugation alone does not
identify these modules
([[thm-dj-bridge-murphy-cell-is-the-same-shape-specht-dual]],
[[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]]). At
$q=1$, $\theta(\sigma)=\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\sigma$, so these identities
contain tensoring with sign; in characteristic $2$ the sign twist becomes
trivial at $q=1$
([[cor-dj-bridge-specialization-and-composition-multiplicity-dictionary]]).
The nonzero quotients in this signed normalization have $e$-regular labels
because the nonzero Murphy quotients have conjugate $e$-restricted labels
([[def-e-regular-and-e-restricted-partitions]]). No generic root-of-unity
Hecke claim is inferred from the published prime-characteristic group-only sign
dictionary, and no semisimplicity or choice principle is assumed.

Let $F$ be a field and $A$ a finite-dimensional unital cellular $F$-algebra with
cellular basis $(C,\Lambda)$ over the finite poset $\Lambda$
([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]). For $\lambda\in\Lambda$
put $D^{\lambda}:=C^{\lambda}/\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$, where
$\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$ is the radical of the cell form
([[lem-cell-form-is-associative-and-its-radical-is-a-submodule]]). Then:

1. if $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ then $D^{\lambda}$ is an absolutely irreducible
   (absolutely simple) $A$-module: it is simple over $F$ and remains simple
   after every extension of scalars to a larger field;
2. $\{D^{\lambda}:\lambda\in\Lambda,\ D^{\lambda}\ne0\}$ is a complete set of
   pairwise non-isomorphic simple $A$-modules ([[def-simple-module]],
   [[thm-jordan-holder-theorem-for-modules]]);
3. $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ if and only if the cell form
   $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_\lambda$ is not identically zero, if and only if
   $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}\ne C^{\lambda}$; and, when these equivalent
   conditions hold, $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$ is the unique maximal proper
   submodule and the Jacobson radical of $C^{\lambda}$, so $D^{\lambda}$ is its
   simple head. If the form is identically zero, the cell-form quotient
   $D^{\lambda}$ is zero; no assertion about the Jacobson radical or the actual
   head of $C^{\lambda}$ is made.

No semisimplicity of $A$ is assumed; the theorem is the Graham-Lehrer
classification and applies in particular to $A=H_{F,q}(S_n)$ for every field
$F$ and every $q\in F^{\times}$.

Let $F$ be a field, $q\in F^{\times}$, let
$e=e(F,q)\in\{2,3,\dots\}\cup\{\infty\}$ be the quantum characteristic
([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]) and let
$H=H_{F,q}(S_n)$ for $n\ge0$. For $\lambda\vdash n$ let $S^{\lambda}$ be the
Hecke Specht module and $D^{\lambda}=S^{\lambda}/\mathrm{rad}\,S^{\lambda}$ its
cell-form quotient ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]). Then:

1. $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ if and only if $\lambda$ is $e$-regular
   ([[def-e-regular-and-e-restricted-partitions]]);
2. $\{D^{\lambda}:\lambda\vdash n\text{ is }e\text{-regular}\}$ is a complete
   set of pairwise non-isomorphic absolutely irreducible $H$-modules;
3. $H$ is split semisimple if and only if $e>n$ (including $e=\infty$); when
   $e\le n$ the algebra has nonzero radical.

This is the exact root-of-unity replacement for the ordinary Specht
classification. At $q=1$ in characteristic $p>0$ it specialises to the
classification of the simple $F[S_n]$-modules by $p$-regular partitions
([[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]]). No
semisimplicity is assumed and no choice principle is used.

Let $p$ be a prime, let $n\ge0$, and let $(K,\mathcal O,k)$ be a splitting
$p$-modular system for $S_n$, so that $k$ is a splitting field of
characteristic $p$ for $S_n$
([[def-splitting-p-modular-system-for-a-finite-group]]). For $\mu\vdash n$
write $S^\mu_k=k\otimes_{\mathbb Z}S^\mu_{\mathbb Z}$ for the field-valued
Specht module, $D^\mu=S^\mu_k/R^\mu$ for its modular form quotient
([[def-modular-specht-form-and-radical-quotient]]), and let
$$S(\mu):=(S^\mu_k)^*=\operatorname{Hom}_k(S^\mu_k,k),\qquad (\sigma\cdot f)(x):=f(\sigma^{-1}x)$$
be the **dual Specht module**, with
$$D(\mu):=\operatorname{hd}\bigl(S(\mu)\bigr) =S(\mu)/\operatorname{rad}\bigl(S(\mu)\bigr)$$
its head ([[def-module-radical-socle-head-and-loewy-series]]). Let
$\mu'$ be the conjugate partition, and let
$S^{\mu'}_k\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$ be the tensor product of
$k[S_n]$-modules with the diagonal action
$\sigma\cdot(x\otimes w)=(\sigma\cdot x)\otimes(\sigma\cdot w)$, where
$\operatorname{sgn}$ is the one-dimensional sign representation
([[def-sign-representation-and-restriction-of-a-representation]],
[[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]).

1. **Dual Specht versus sign-twisted conjugate.** If $\mu$ is $p$-restricted
   (equivalently, by
   [[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]], $\mu'$ is $p$-regular),
   then $S(\mu)\cong S^{\mu'}_k\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$; consequently
   $S(\mu)$ is nonzero with simple head
   $$D(\mu)\cong D^{\mu'}\otimes\operatorname{sgn},$$
   a nonzero simple $k[S_n]$-module that is self-dual and absolutely
   irreducible.
2. **Equivalent form for $p$-regular labels.** If $\lambda\vdash n$ is
   $p$-regular, then $\lambda'$ is $p$-restricted and
   $$D^\lambda\cong D(\lambda')\otimes\operatorname{sgn}.$$
3. **The two labellings.** The map $\mu\mapsto D(\mu)$ is a bijection from
   the set of $p$-restricted partitions of $n$ to the set of isomorphism
   classes of simple $k[S_n]$-modules; that is, every simple
   $k[S_n]$-module is isomorphic to $D(\mu)$ for exactly one $p$-restricted
   $\mu\vdash n$.

In characteristic $2$ the sign representation is the trivial representation,
so the formulas read $D(\mu)\cong D^{\mu'}$ and $D^\lambda\cong D(\lambda')$;
the transposition is still required, and the two labellings coincide only
for self-conjugate partitions. No step divides by a group order or uses
averaging, and $n=0$ is included.

derivations.claim: Weyl modules: multiplying by $e=\varphi_{t^{\omega}t^{\omega}}$ kills every semistandard basis element whose type is not $\omega$; for type $\omega$ the surviving basis elements $\varphi_T$ are exactly those indexed by standard $\lambda$-tableaux, and the resulting corner $W^{\lambda}e$ is free on the Murphy basis of the Hecke cell module $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$, giving $F(W^{\lambda})\cong S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$. This is part (1) for Weyl modules.

Forms: the product $\varphi_{T^{\lambda},s}\varphi_{t,T^{\lambda}}$, evaluated at $m_{\lambda}$, is the Murphy product $m_{t^{\lambda}s}m_{t\,t^{\lambda}}$, and higher Schur shapes evaluate to higher Murphy shapes; the scalar coefficient therefore identifies the form on $W^{\lambda}e$ with the cell form on $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$. Since $e^*=e$, associativity makes $W^{\lambda}e$ orthogonal to $W^{\lambda}(1-e)$, so $\mathrm{rad}(W^{\lambda})e=\mathrm{rad}(W^{\lambda}e)$; the Weyl form is nonzero because the canonical semistandard projection has Gram value $1$, and by [F3] the quotient $L^{\lambda}=W^{\lambda}/\mathrm{rad}(W^{\lambda})$ is the unique simple head. Exactness of $F$ now gives $F(L^{\lambda})\cong S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}/\mathrm{rad}(S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M})=D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$, including the zero-form case. This completes part (1).

Nonvanishing: by the source's nonvanishing criterion recorded in [F4] the quotient $D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ is nonzero exactly for $e$-restricted $\lambda$; by step 2.1 this is exactly the nonvanishing condition for $F(L^{\lambda})$. This is part (2).

Dictionary: replacing $\lambda$ by $\lambda'$ and using $S^{\lambda}=(S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta$, $D^{\lambda}=(D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta$ from [F2] turns parts (1)-(3) into the stated Dipper-James dictionary, with the conjugation of labels supplied by [F5] and the same involutive pullback applied to both sides, which preserves composition multiplicities because $\theta$ is an algebra automorphism.

boundaries.evidence: Part 2 is the exact non-vanishing statement F(L^lambda)=0 precisely when lambda is not e-restricted; when no e-restricted nu exists the multiplicity statement of part 3 is vacuous.
Step 1.1 shows F(W^lambda) has the surviving semistandard basis elements with standard index, so F(W^lambda) is nonzero, while part 2 locates the zero images among the simple modules.

Step 1.1's surviving basis of F(W^lambda) has one element for the one-dimensional shapes (n) and (1^n), and step 4.1 applies the functor termwise to a composition series without losing the single-factor cases.
The degenerate weight omega=(1^n) is exactly what the idempotent e projects onto: step 1.1 multiplies by e and kills every basis element whose type is not omega.

boundaries.reason: The parameters are integers with d>=n and lambda in the finite set Lambda^+(d,n); no interval endpoint, limit or boundary value occurs in the theorem.

boundaries.evidence: The Statement records that no choice is used; F is built from the fixed idempotent e and steps 1.1-4.1 apply it to fixed bases and composition series.
Part 2's forward direction, F(L^lambda) nonzero implies lambda e-restricted, is step 3.1 read through the source's nonvanishing criterion recorded in [F4].
Part 2's reverse direction, lambda e-restricted implies F(L^lambda) nonzero, is the other half of the same criterion in step 3.1.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^{\times}$, $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$, and let
$L_1,\dots,L_n$ be the Hecke Jucys-Murphy elements
([[def-hecke-jucys-murphy-elements-and-q-contents]]). For every $\lambda\vdash n$,
every standard $\lambda$-tableau $t$ and every $1\le k\le n$ there exist
$a_v\in R$ with
$$m_tL_k=[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q\,m_t+\sum_{v\rhd t}a_v\,m_v,$$
where $(m_t)_{t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)}$ is the Murphy basis of the Murphy cell
module $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$
([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]) and the sum is over standard
$\lambda$-tableaux $v$ strictly dominating $t$ in the dominance order on
tableaux ([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]],
[[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]). In particular $L_k$ acts on
the Murphy cell module $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ with Murphy basis $(m_t)$ by a
triangular matrix whose diagonal entries are the q-content values.
Consequently the $L_k$ commute pairwise and every symmetric polynomial in
$L_1,\dots,L_n$ is central in $H$.

Let $F$ be a field and $q\in F^{\times}$ an invertible element. The **quantum
characteristic** $e=e(F,q)$ is the least integer $e\ge2$ such that
$1+q+\cdots+q^{e-1}=0$ in $F$, and $e:=\infty$ when no such integer exists
([[def-q-integer-q-factorial-and-q-multinomial]],
[[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Since $[1]_q=1\ne0$, the least positive
integer $e$ with $[e]_q=0$, when it exists, automatically satisfies $e\ge2$, so
the two formulations coincide.

Concretely: (i) if $q\ne1$ then $[m]_q=(q^m-1)/(q-1)$ for all $m\ge0$ — indeed
$(q-1)(1+q+\cdots+q^{m-1})=q^m-1$ and $q-1\ne0$ — so $[e]_q=0$ is equivalent
to $q^e=1$, and a finite $e$ exists exactly when $q$ is a root of unity and
then $e$ is the multiplicative order of $q$ in $F^{\times}$ (which is $\ge2$
because $q\ne1$); (ii) if $q=1$ then $[m]_1=m$, so $e=\operatorname{char}(F)$
when $\operatorname{char}(F)>0$ (the characteristic is a prime, hence at least
$2$, and $m\cdot1_F\ne0$ for $1\le m<p$) and $e=\infty$ when
$\operatorname{char}(F)=0$
([[prop-group-algebra-and-finite-field-specializations-of-the-generic-hecke-algebra]]).

If $e<\infty$ then $q\ne1$ implies $q^e=1$, and hence $[m+e]_q=[m]_q$ for
every integer $m$: for $m\ge0$ the sum splits as
$$[m+e]_q=[m]_q+q^m[e]_q,$$
so $[m+e]_q=[m]_q$ whenever $[e]_q=0$; for the remaining $m<0$ one extends the
closed formula by $[m]_q:=(q^m-1)/(q-1)$ when $q\ne1$ and reads $[m]_1:=m\in F$
for the canonical image of the integer $m$ when $q=1$, in which case
$e=\operatorname{char}(F)$ and $[m+e]_1=m+e=m$ in $F$. In particular the
quantum characteristic, not merely the multiplicative order, is the parameter
governing the modular representation theory of the Hecke algebra. No choice
principle is used.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $q\in R^{\times}$. With the Murphy cellular
basis $(\mathcal M,\Lambda)$ of $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$
([[thm-murphy-tableau-elements-form-a-cellular-basis]],
[[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]) and the canonical tableau
$t^\lambda$ of shape $\lambda\vdash n$
([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]]), the **Murphy cell
module** $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ is the right cell module $C^{\lambda}$ of the
Murphy basis: it is the free $R$-module with basis
$\{m_t:=m_{t^\lambda t}:t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)\}$ - the classes of the
Murphy elements whose *first* index is the canonical tableau - and $H$ acts by
$m_th=\sum_vr_vm_v$ whenever
$m_{t^\lambda t}h\equiv\sum_vr_vm_{t^\lambda v}\pmod{H^{\rhd\lambda}}$. (The
cellular action rule transforms the second index and fixes the first, so the
diagonal elements $m_{tt}$ alone do not span a submodule; the module basis is
the fixed-first-index family above.) Its **cell form** is the unique bilinear
form $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_\lambda:S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}\times
S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}\to R$ with
$$m_{us}m_{tv}\equiv\langle m_s,m_t\rangle_\lambda\,m_{uv}\pmod{H^{\rhd\lambda}}$$
for all $s,t,u,v\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)$; it is symmetric and associative and
$\mathrm{rad}\,S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ is a submodule, so
$D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}:=S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}/\mathrm{rad}\,S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$
is a right $H$-module
([[lem-cell-form-is-associative-and-its-radical-is-a-submodule]]).

**Convention (Dipper-James signed cellular normalization).** Let $\theta:H\to H$
be the involutive algebra automorphism defined by
$\theta(T_i)=-qT_i^{-1}=(q-1)-T_i$
([[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]]). For a right module $M$,
write $M^\theta$ for the same $R$-module with action $x\cdot h=x\theta(h)$. The
page's ordinary Specht normalization is the signed conjugate Murphy
construction
$$S^{\lambda}:=(S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta,$$
where $\lambda'$ is the conjugate partition ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). Its form is the form of
$S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}$ on the same underlying module; because $\theta$
commutes with $*$ this is associative for the twisted action
([[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]]). Over a field put
$$D^{\lambda}:=S^{\lambda}/\operatorname{rad}_{\rm form}S^{\lambda}=(D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta.$$
Thus $S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}=(S^{\lambda})^\theta$ and
$D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}=(D^{\lambda})^\theta$; conjugation alone does not
identify these modules
([[thm-dj-bridge-murphy-cell-is-the-same-shape-specht-dual]],
[[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]]). At
$q=1$, $\theta(\sigma)=\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\sigma$, so these identities
contain tensoring with sign; in characteristic $2$ the sign twist becomes
trivial at $q=1$
([[cor-dj-bridge-specialization-and-composition-multiplicity-dictionary]]).
The nonzero quotients in this signed normalization have $e$-regular labels
because the nonzero Murphy quotients have conjugate $e$-restricted labels
([[def-e-regular-and-e-restricted-partitions]]). No generic root-of-unity
Hecke claim is inferred from the published prime-characteristic group-only sign
dictionary, and no semisimplicity or choice principle is assumed.

derivations.claim: Separation of contents: because $e>n$, two nodes of $[\,\lambda\,]$ that are distinct and have the same residue lie neither in the same row nor in the same column, and distinct removable nodes have distinct residues ([F2] applied to the contents of the nodes removed in the order $n,n-1,\dots,1$); peeling off the nodes carrying $n,n-1,\dots,1$ therefore reconstructs $t$ from its q-content sequence, giving the first claim of (1). The same argument for fixed $i$ shows that the pair $(s,t=s(i\ i+1))$ is the only possible source of a common sequence when one coordinate is allowed to disagree.

Combined case: when $i,i+1$ lie in the same row of $s$ the defining relation $T_iL_i=L_iT_i$ together with the content computation gives $T_i$-eigenvalue $q$; when they lie in the same column the eigenvalue is $-1$; both are the standard row and column cases of the Hecke generator action, and the stated values follow from $m_sT_i=m_s$ and $m_sT_i=-m_s$ respectively in the Murphy basis.

Spectral projectors: the $L_k$ commute by [F1], so $F_t$ is a well-defined element of the commutative algebra $F[L_1,\dots,L_n]$; all denominators are nonzero by step 1.1. On the basis vector $m_v$, the triangularity [F1] gives $m_vL_k=[\operatorname{content}_v(k)]_q\,m_v+(\text{more dominant})$; differentiating the tableaux by their content sequences shows that $F_t$ kills every $m_v$ with $v\rhd t$ (some factor $L_k-[\operatorname{content}_v(k)]_q$ with $[\operatorname{content}_v(k)]_q\ne[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q$ vanishes on the eigenvalue of $v$), while $F_t$ acts as the identity on the t-eigenspace. Hence $f_t=m_t+\sum_{s\rhd t}a_sm_s$ and $f_tL_k=[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q f_t$. This is part (2).

Orthogonality and the basis: the $F_t$, for the distinct content sequences of step 1.1, are orthogonal Lagrange projectors in $F[L_1,\dots,L_n]$, so $F_sF_t=\delta_{st}F_s$ and $f_sF_t=m_sF_sF_t=\delta_{st}f_s$, giving part of (3). For the form: by [F3] and the self-adjointness $L_k^*=L_k$, for $s\ne t$ and any $k$ with $[\operatorname{content}_s(k)]_q\ne[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q$ one has $${[\operatorname{content}}_s(k)]_q\langle f_s,f_t\rangle_\lambda=\langle f_sL_k,f_t\rangle_\lambda=\langle f_s,f_tL_k\rangle_\lambda=[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q\langle f_s,f_t\rangle_\lambda,$$ hence $\langle f_s,f_t\rangle_\lambda=0$; this gives the orthogonality, and the transition matrix from $(m_t)$ to $(f_t)$ is unitriangular by step 2.1, hence invertible, giving the basis property. This completes part (3).

Axial computation: otherwise $t=s(i\ i+1)$ is standard and, by parts (1)-(3), $f_sT_i$ is an eigenvector of each $L_k$ with $k\ne i,i+1$ with the content of $s$ (equivalently of $t$); separation forces $f_sT_i\in\operatorname{span}(f_s,f_t)$. Write $f_sT_i=\alpha_i(s)f_t+c_sf_s$. Multiplying the relation $T_iL_i=T_iL_{i+1}-1-(q-1)L_{i+1}$ (an elementary consequence of the definition of the $L_k$ and the Hecke relations) on the left by $f_s$ and using the eigenvalues gives $c_s=-1/[\rho]_q$. Applying $T_i$ twice and using the quadratic relation $T_i^2=(q-1)T_i+q$ gives $\alpha_i(s)\alpha_i(t)=[1+\rho]_q[1-\rho]_q/([\rho]_q[-\rho]_q)$; since $\operatorname{content}_t(i)-\operatorname{content}_t(i+1)=-\rho$, the dominance cases are $\rho>0$ with $s\rhd t$ and $\rho<0$ with $t\rhd s$, yielding the two displayed branches. This is part (4).

Assembly: steps 1.1, 1.2, 2.1, 3.1 and 4.1 prove the four parts; no semisimplicity of $H$ was used, since the construction takes place in the commutative subalgebra generated by the $L_k$ and only uses the triangularity on the cell module, and no choice principle is used.

boundaries.evidence: For a shape with a single standard tableau, and for n=0, part 1 of the Statement is vacuous and the product defining F_t is empty, giving F_t=1 and f_t=m_t in the seminormal construction.
The denominators of F_t are nonzero exactly by part 1 (step 1.1), and part 4's term -1/[rho]_q is legitimate because |rho|<=n-1<e; step 5.1 records that no semisimplicity is assumed.
The projector f_t=m_t+sum over s strictly dominating t of a_s m_s has the single leading term m_t, and step 4.1 computes the generator action for t=s(i i+1) directly.
Degenerate residue collisions are excluded by the hypothesis e>n: step 1.1 shows distinct same-residue nodes share neither a row nor a column and distinct removable nodes have distinct residues.

boundaries.reason: The parameter e satisfies e>n (infinity allowed) and the remaining data are finite sets of standard tableaux; no interval, limiting process or extremal endpoint occurs.

boundaries.evidence: The Statement's final sentence records that no choice principle is used; the construction lives in the commutative algebra F[L_1,...,L_n] generated by the fixed elements L_k.

boundaries.reason: The theorem's four parts are separation, a projector construction, orthogonality and a generator formula; none is the forward half of a biconditional.
No converse is claimed; in particular the theorem does not assert that equality in the generator formula characterises the seminormal projectors.

Let $R$ be an integral domain, $q\in R^{\times}$, $d,n\ge1$, and let $S(d,n)$
be the q-Schur algebra with Weyl modules $W^{\lambda}$
([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). For a partition $\lambda$ of
$n$ with at most $d$ parts and a weight (composition of $n$ with at most $d$
parts) $\mu$, let $G^{\lambda}_{\mu}\in R$ be the determinant of the Gram matrix
of the cell form of $W^{\lambda}$ restricted to its $\mu$-weight space, computed
with respect to the semistandard basis. Let
$\beta=\beta(\lambda)=(\beta_1,\dots,\beta_n)$ be the beta sequence
$\beta_i=\lambda'_i+n-i$ of $\lambda$
([[def-alternating-weyl-and-specht-symbols-from-beta-sequences]],
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]) and let
$h^{\lambda}_{ab}=\lambda_a-b+\lambda'_b-a+1$ be the hook length of the node
$(a,b)\in[\lambda]$, with leg length $l^{\lambda}_{ab}$
([[def-hook-arm-leg-and-hook-length]]). Then
$$G^{\lambda}_{\mu}=q^{N}\prod_{\substack{(a,b),(a,c)\in[\lambda]\\ b<c}}\left(\frac{[h^{\lambda}_{ab}]_q}{[h^{\lambda}_{ac}]_q}\right)^{d_{\mu}(\beta_1,\dots,\beta_b+h^{\lambda}_{ab},\dots,\beta_c-h^{\lambda}_{ac},\dots,\beta_n)},$$
where $N=N(\lambda,\mu)$ is the explicit integer
$\sum_T\ell(d(\mathrm{last}(T)))$ summed over the semistandard
$\lambda$-tableaux $T$ of type $\mu$ (the degree of the corresponding
semistandard basis vector), $d_{\mu}$ is the signed semistandard multiplicity
of [[def-alternating-weyl-and-specht-symbols-from-beta-sequences]] and
$[\ ]_q$ are the quantum integers
([[def-q-integer-q-factorial-and-q-multinomial]]). The exponent has the exact
combinatorial interpretation of Lemma 5.26:
$$d_{\mu}(\beta_1,\dots,\beta_b+h^{\lambda}_{ab},\dots,\beta_c-h^{\lambda}_{ac},\dots,\beta_n)=(-1)^{l^{\lambda}_{ab}+l^{\lambda}_{ac}}\,|T_0(\eta,\mu)|$$
whenever $\eta$ is obtained from $\lambda$ by unwrapping the removable border
strip $R^{\lambda}_{ac}$ (the hook of $(a,c)$, of size $h^{\lambda}_{ac}$) and
re-wrapping it with its lowest node in column $b$, and it is zero otherwise
([[def-removable-border-strip-and-height]],
[[lem-hooks-correspond-to-removable-border-strips]]). The product is
interpreted in $R$ after pairing all numerator and denominator factors, so the
displayed formula represents an element of $R$ even though individual factors
need not be units, and the theorem is stated over an integral domain, not only
over a field.

In the setting of [[def-jantzen-filtration-of-a-lifted-cell-module]] ($R$ a PID,
$\pi$ a prime element, $F=R/\pi R$, $M$ free of finite rank with a form whose
extension to $K=\operatorname{Frac}(R)$ is non-degenerate), let $\nu_\pi$ be
the $\pi$-adic valuation normalised by $\nu_\pi(\pi)=1$ and let
$G\in R\setminus\{0\}$ be the Gram determinant of the form with respect to any
$R$-basis of $M$. Then
$$\nu_\pi(G)=\sum_{i>0}\dim_FM_F(i),$$
where $M_F(i)$ are the Jantzen layers of
[[def-jantzen-filtration-of-a-lifted-cell-module]]; in particular the sum is
finite and independent of the chosen basis.

Let $F$ be a field, $q\in F^{\times}$, $d,n\ge1$, and let $S=S(d,n)$ be the
q-Schur algebra with Weyl modules $W^{\lambda}$ for
$\lambda\in\Lambda^{+}(d,n)$
([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). Let $M$ be a
finite-dimensional right $S$-module and let $(a_{\lambda})_{\lambda\in\Lambda^{+}(d,n)}$
be integers such that
$$\dim_F\bigl(M\varphi_{T^{\nu}T^{\nu}}\bigr)=\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda^{+}(d,n)}a_{\lambda}\,\dim_F\bigl(W^{\lambda}\varphi_{T^{\nu}T^{\nu}}\bigr)$$
for every partition $\nu\in\Lambda^{+}(d,n)$, where $\varphi_{T^{\nu}T^{\nu}}$
are the diagonal semistandard basis elements
([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). Then
$[M]=\sum_{\lambda}a_{\lambda}[W^{\lambda}]$ in the Grothendieck group
$G_0(S\text{-mod})$
([[def-grothendieck-group-of-an-essentially-small-abelian-category]]).
Consequently equality of all semistandard weight-space dimensions forces
equality in the Grothendieck group.

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ be a partition with English Young diagram $[\lambda]$, so
that rows are numbered downward and columns rightward, and let
$\nu\subseteq\lambda$ be a subpartition, so that the skew diagram
$[\lambda/\nu]=[\lambda]\setminus[\nu]$ is the set of nodes of $[\lambda]$
outside $[\nu]$ ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]],
[[def-skew-diagram-and-semistandard-skew-tableau]]). Two nodes are
side-adjacent when their coordinates differ by exactly one in exactly one
coordinate.

A **removable border strip** of $\lambda$ (also called a **skew hook** or
**rim hook**) is a nonempty set $\xi$ of nodes of $[\lambda]$ such that

(i) $\xi$ is **edge-connected**: any two nodes of $\xi$ are joined by a chain
of side-adjacent nodes of $\xi$;

(ii) $\xi$ contains **no $2\times2$ block**: there are no nodes
$(i,j),(i+1,j),(i,j+1),(i+1,j+1)$ all belonging to $\xi$;

(iii) $[\lambda]\setminus\xi$ is again the Young diagram of a partition, say
$[\lambda]\setminus\xi=[\nu]$ for a partition $\nu\vdash n-|\xi|$.

Equivalently, a removable border strip is a skew diagram $\lambda/\nu$ that is
connected and contains no $2\times2$ block; since the complement of
$[\lambda/\nu]$ in $[\lambda]$ is $[\nu]$, condition (iii) is then automatic,
and (i) and (ii) say exactly that the skew diagram is connected and free of
$2\times2$ blocks. We write $\xi=\lambda/\nu$ in that case. The **size** of
$\xi$ is its number of nodes $|\xi|$; a removable border strip of size $r$ is a
**removable $r$-strip**, and then $\nu\vdash n-r$.

The **height** (also **leg length**) of a nonempty connected border strip
$\xi$ is
$$\operatorname{ht}(\xi):=(\text{number of distinct rows of }[\lambda]\text{ occupied by }\xi)-1.$$

**The counting identity.** If a removable border strip $\xi$ has $r$ nodes and
occupies $c$ distinct columns and $w$ distinct rows of $[\lambda]$, then
$w=r-c+1$, hence $\operatorname{ht}(\xi)=r-c\ge0$. Indeed $[\lambda/\nu]$ is a
connected skew diagram with complement a Young diagram, so all its nodes lie
on the rim of $[\lambda]$, the set of nodes $(p,q)$ with
$(p+1,q+1)\notin[\lambda]$, and form a path that moves only downward or
rightward: each node after the first is reached from its predecessor by one
downward step or one rightward step. The $r-1$ steps consist of $w-1$ downward
steps and $c-1$ rightward steps, since the path visits exactly the $w$
occupied rows and exactly the $c$ occupied columns, whence
$r-1=(w-1)+(c-1)$.

In particular $\operatorname{ht}(\xi)=0$ exactly when $\xi$ is a horizontal
strip, that is, occupies at most one node in each column, and in general
$c=r-\operatorname{ht}(\xi)$ is the number of columns occupied. A removable
border strip of size $1$ is exactly a removable node
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]]): a single node is
edge-connected and contains no $2\times2$ block, and its removal leaves a Young
diagram precisely when the node is removable. No choice principle is used.

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ and $x=(i,j)\in[\lambda]$. Let $H(x)$ be the hook of $x$,
with arm length $a(x)=\lambda_i-j$, leg length $\ell(x)=\lambda'_j-i$ and hook
length $h(x)=a(x)+\ell(x)+1$
([[def-hook-arm-leg-and-hook-length]]); its two endpoints are the last node
$(i,\lambda_i)$ of its arm and the last node $(\lambda'_j,j)$ of its leg. Let
$\xi(x)$ be the unique edge-connected set of nodes of $[\lambda]$ with
endpoints $(i,\lambda_i)$ and $(\lambda'_j,j)$ that lies in the rim of
$[\lambda]$, i.e. consists of nodes $(p,q)$ with $(p+1,q+1)\notin[\lambda]$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]],
[[def-skew-diagram-and-semistandard-skew-tableau]]). Then:

1. $\xi(x)$ is a removable border strip of $\lambda$ of size $h(x)$ and height
   $\ell(x)$ ([[def-removable-border-strip-and-height]]), and
   $[\lambda]\setminus\xi(x)$ is a Young diagram, so $\lambda\setminus\xi(x)$ is
   a partition of $n-h(x)$;

   node $x\in[\lambda]$; hence $x\mapsto\xi(x)$ is a bijection from the nodes

Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$, let $q\in R^{\times}$, let $d,n\ge0$
with $d\ge n$, and let $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Write
$S:=S(d,n)=\mathrm{End}_H(M)$ for the type-A q-Schur algebra with
$M=\bigoplus_{\mu\in\Lambda(d,n)}M^{\mu}$ the direct sum of the permutation
modules ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]],
[[def-direct-sum-of-a-family-of-modules]]) and let
$\{\varphi_{ST}:\lambda\in\Lambda^{+}(d,n),\ S,T\in T_0(\lambda)\}$ be its
cellular semistandard basis ([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]]
for the underlying Murphy elements and
[[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]] for the standard
basis along which this basis is defined). Put
$\omega:=(1^n)\in\Lambda(d,n)$, the composition with $n$ parts equal to $1$
(legitimate because $d\ge n$), so that the Young subgroup $S_\omega$ is trivial
and $m_\omega=1$; hence
$$M^{\omega}=m_\omega H=H$$
is the regular right $H$-module. Let $t^{\omega}$ be the unique standard
$\omega$-tableau, with entries $1,2,\dots,n$ down its single column; it is in
particular the unique row-standard $\omega$-tableau whose entries increase down
the column. Set
$$e:=\varphi_{t^{\omega}t^{\omega}}\in S.$$

Then:

1. $e$ is the projection of $M$ onto the direct summand $M^{\omega}=H$ along
   the other summands $M^{\mu}$, $\mu\ne\omega$; in particular $e^2=e$ and
   $$eSe\cong\mathrm{End}_H(M^{\omega})=\mathrm{End}_H(H),$$ via the algebra
   isomorphism
   $$\rho:H\longrightarrow eSe,\qquad h\longmapsto\rho_h,\qquad \rho_h(x):=hx,$$
   left multiplication by $h$ on $M^{\omega}=H$ being a right $H$-module
   endomorphism. Here the isomorphism $eSe\cong\mathrm{End}_H(M^{\omega})$
   sends $efe$ to $f|_{M^{\omega}}$ and is inverted by extending an
   endomorphism of $M^{\omega}$ by zero on the other summands, and the
   identification $\mathrm{End}_H(H)\cong H$ sends an endomorphism to its value
   at $1$. By the construction of the semistandard basis elements $\varphi_{ST}$
   (Mathas (4.13) with Corollaries 4.9 and 4.12; see the locator above), the
   diagonal element $\varphi_{t^{\omega}t^{\omega}}$ is exactly the
   endomorphism of $M$ that is the identity on $M^{\omega}$ and zero on all
   $M^{\mu}$ with $\mu\ne\omega$, which is the projection asserted above.
2. The **Schur functor** is
   $$F:\mathrm{mod}\text{-}S\longrightarrow\mathrm{mod}\text{-}H,\qquad F(X):=Xe=X\otimes_SSe,$$
   with the right $H$-action transported along $\rho$, so that
   $(xe)\cdot h:=x\,\rho_h$ for $x\in X$, $h\in H$
   ([[def-left-and-right-modules]]). It is exact and $R$-linear on morphisms:
   since $e^2=e$, the right $S$-module $Se$ is a direct summand of the regular
   right $S$-module $S$, so $X\mapsto X\otimes_SSe$ is a direct summand of the
   identity functor $X\mapsto X\otimes_SS\cong X$, which is exact; equivalently,
   right multiplication by $e$ is a direct-summand projection on underlying
   $R$-modules and the functor is a composition of the exact functors
   $X\mapsto X\otimes_SS$ and the idempotent projection $X\mapsto Xe$. The
   convention is fixed: the functor is $X\mapsto Xe$ on the right, and the
   left-module formula $X\mapsto eX$ is not used on this page.

functor of [[def-schur-idempotent-and-schur-functor-for-type-a-q-schur-algebras]].

$L^{\lambda}$ its simple head
([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). Then, in the source's
(dual-Specht) normalisation:

1. $F(W^{\lambda})\cong S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{M}}$ and
   $F(L^{\lambda})\cong D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{M}}$ as right $H$-modules (where
   $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{M}}$, $D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{M}}$ are the source's cell
   module and its cell-form quotient, which is its simple head when nonzero);
2. $F(L^{\lambda})\ne0$ if and only if $\lambda$ is $e$-restricted; and
3. for every $e$-restricted $\nu\vdash n$ one has

([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]) the dictionary reads:

$[W^{\lambda'}:L^{\nu'}]=[S^{\lambda}:D^{\nu}]$ for $e$-regular $\nu$; the

[[prop-p-regular-and-p-restricted-simple-labels-are-related-by-conjugate-sign-duality]].

used.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^{\times}$, and $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). For $1\le k\le n$ define
$$L_1:=0,\qquad L_k:=q^{-1}T_{(k-1,k)}+q^{-2}T_{(k-2,k)}+\cdots+q^{1-k}T_{(1,k)}\in H\quad(k\ge2),$$
where $T_{(i,k)}$ is the standard basis element indexed by the transposition
$(i\ k)$ ([[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). The $L_k$
are the **Hecke Jucys-Murphy elements**. They are fixed by the star
anti-automorphism $T_w^*=T_{w^{-1}}$
([[lem-the-star-antiautomorphism-of-the-type-a-hecke-algebra]]): each
transposition $(i\ k)$ is its own inverse, so $T_{(i,k)}^*=T_{(i,k)}$, and the
coefficients $q^{i-k}$ are central, whence
$L_k^*=\sum_{i<k}q^{i-k}T_{(i,k)}=L_k$. They commute pairwise and every
symmetric polynomial in $L_1,\dots,L_n$ with coefficients in $R$ is central in
$H$ ([[thm-hecke-jucys-murphy-action-is-dominance-triangular]]).

**q-contents.** The quantum integers $[m]_q$ for $m\ge0$ are those of
[[def-q-integer-q-factorial-and-q-multinomial]]; extend the definition to
negative indices by $[-m]_q:=-q^{-m}[m]_q$ for $m>0$, so that
$[m]_q=(q^m-1)/(q-1)$ for all $m\in\mathbb Z$ when $q\ne1$ — indeed for $m=-r<0$
one has $-q^{-r}(q^r-1)/(q-1)=(q^{-r}-1)/(q-1)$ — and $[m]_1=m$ for all
$m\in\mathbb Z$, since $[-r]_1=-[r]_1=-r$. For a standard $\lambda$-tableau $t$
and $1\le k\le n$ let $\operatorname{content}_t(k)=c-r$ be the content of the
node carrying $k$ ([[def-content-vector-of-a-standard-tableau]]) and define the
**q-content value** $[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q$. If $e=e(F,q)<\infty$ for
a field $F$ then $[m+e]_q=[m]_q$ for every $m\in\mathbb Z$
([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]), so the
q-content value depends only on the residue of the content modulo $e$. At $q=1$
the identification $H_{R,1}(S_n)\cong R[S_n]$ with $T_w\mapsto w$ — the
$R$-linear base change of the specialization isomorphism of
[[prop-group-algebra-and-finite-field-specializations-of-the-generic-hecke-algebra]]
— sends $L_k$ to the ordinary Jucys-Murphy element
$X_k=\sum_{j<k}(j\ k)$
([[def-jucys-murphy-elements-of-the-symmetric-group-algebra]]), because each
coefficient $q^{j-k}$ specializes to $1$, and
$[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_1=\operatorname{content}_t(k)$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^{\times}$, $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$, and let
$L_1,\dots,L_n$ be the Hecke Jucys-Murphy elements
([[def-hecke-jucys-murphy-elements-and-q-contents]]). For every $\lambda\vdash n$,
every standard $\lambda$-tableau $t$ and every $1\le k\le n$ there exist
$a_v\in R$ with
$$m_tL_k=[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q\,m_t+\sum_{v\rhd t}a_v\,m_v,$$
where $(m_t)_{t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)}$ is the Murphy basis of the Murphy cell
module $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$
([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]) and the sum is over standard
$\lambda$-tableaux $v$ strictly dominating $t$ in the dominance order on
tableaux ([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]],
[[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]). In particular $L_k$ acts on
the Murphy cell module $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ with Murphy basis $(m_t)$ by a
triangular matrix whose diagonal entries are the q-content values.
Consequently the $L_k$ commute pairwise and every symmetric polynomial in
$L_1,\dots,L_n$ is central in $H$.

Let $F$ be a field and $q\in F^{\times}$ an invertible element. The **quantum
characteristic** $e=e(F,q)$ is the least integer $e\ge2$ such that
$1+q+\cdots+q^{e-1}=0$ in $F$, and $e:=\infty$ when no such integer exists
([[def-q-integer-q-factorial-and-q-multinomial]],
[[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Since $[1]_q=1\ne0$, the least positive
integer $e$ with $[e]_q=0$, when it exists, automatically satisfies $e\ge2$, so
the two formulations coincide.

Concretely: (i) if $q\ne1$ then $[m]_q=(q^m-1)/(q-1)$ for all $m\ge0$ — indeed
$(q-1)(1+q+\cdots+q^{m-1})=q^m-1$ and $q-1\ne0$ — so $[e]_q=0$ is equivalent
to $q^e=1$, and a finite $e$ exists exactly when $q$ is a root of unity and
then $e$ is the multiplicative order of $q$ in $F^{\times}$ (which is $\ge2$
because $q\ne1$); (ii) if $q=1$ then $[m]_1=m$, so $e=\operatorname{char}(F)$
when $\operatorname{char}(F)>0$ (the characteristic is a prime, hence at least
$2$, and $m\cdot1_F\ne0$ for $1\le m<p$) and $e=\infty$ when
$\operatorname{char}(F)=0$
([[prop-group-algebra-and-finite-field-specializations-of-the-generic-hecke-algebra]]).

If $e<\infty$ then $q\ne1$ implies $q^e=1$, and hence $[m+e]_q=[m]_q$ for
every integer $m$: for $m\ge0$ the sum splits as
$$[m+e]_q=[m]_q+q^m[e]_q,$$
so $[m+e]_q=[m]_q$ whenever $[e]_q=0$; for the remaining $m<0$ one extends the
closed formula by $[m]_q:=(q^m-1)/(q-1)$ when $q\ne1$ and reads $[m]_1:=m\in F$
for the canonical image of the integer $m$ when $q=1$, in which case
$e=\operatorname{char}(F)$ and $[m+e]_1=m+e=m$ in $F$. In particular the
quantum characteristic, not merely the multiplicative order, is the parameter
governing the modular representation theory of the Hecke algebra. No choice
principle is used.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^{\times}$, and $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). For $1\le k\le n$ define

where $T_{(i,k)}$ is the standard basis element indexed by the transposition

**q-contents.** The quantum integers $[m]_q$ for $m\ge0$ are those of
[[def-q-integer-q-factorial-and-q-multinomial]]; extend the definition to
negative indices by $[-m]_q:=-q^{-m}[m]_q$ for $m>0$, so that
$[m]_q=(q^m-1)/(q-1)$ for all $m\in\mathbb Z$ when $q\ne1$ — indeed for $m=-r<0$
one has $-q^{-r}(q^r-1)/(q-1)=(q^{-r}-1)/(q-1)$ — and $[m]_1=m$ for all
$m\in\mathbb Z$, since $[-r]_1=-[r]_1=-r$. For a standard $\lambda$-tableau $t$
and $1\le k\le n$ let $\operatorname{content}_t(k)=c-r$ be the content of the
node carrying $k$ ([[def-content-vector-of-a-standard-tableau]]) and define the
**q-content value** $[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q$. If $e=e(F,q)<\infty$ for

([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]), so the
q-content value depends only on the residue of the content modulo $e$. At $q=1$
the identification $H_{R,1}(S_n)\cong R[S_n]$ with $T_w\mapsto w$ — the
$R$-linear base change of the specialization isomorphism of
[[prop-group-algebra-and-finite-field-specializations-of-the-generic-hecke-algebra]]
— sends $L_k$ to the ordinary Jucys-Murphy element
$X_k=\sum_{j<k}(j\ k)$
([[def-jucys-murphy-elements-of-the-symmetric-group-algebra]]), because each
coefficient $q^{j-k}$ specializes to $1$, and
$[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_1=\operatorname{content}_t(k)$.

Let $F$ be a field, $q\in F^{\times}$, let $e=e(F,q)$ and assume $e>n$ (with
$e=\infty$ allowed); let $\lambda\vdash n$, $H=H_{F,q}(S_n)$, and let
$S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ be the Murphy cell module with Murphy basis
$(m_t)_{t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)}$
([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]).

1. (**Separation**) If $s,t$ are standard $\lambda$-tableaux with
   $[\operatorname{content}_s(k)]_q=[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q$ for all
   $1\le k\le n$ then $s=t$. More precisely, if the q-content values agree for
   all $k\notin\{i,i+1\}$ for some $i$, then $s=t$ or $t=s(i\ i+1)$.
2. (**Idempotents**) For a standard $\lambda$-tableau $t$ define, inside the
   commutative algebra $F[L_1,\dots,L_n]$,
   $$F_t:=\prod_{k=1}^{n}\ \prod_{\substack{s\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)\\[2pt] [\operatorname{content}_s(k)]_q\ne[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q}}\frac{L_k-[\operatorname{content}_s(k)]_q}{[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q-[\operatorname{content}_s(k)]_q}$$
   and put $f_t:=m_tF_t\in S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$. All denominators are
   nonzero by (1) and the $f_t$ are well-defined spectral projectors:
   $f_tL_k=[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q\,f_t$, and
   $f_t=m_t+\sum_{s\rhd t}a_sm_s$ for suitable $a_s\in F$.
3. (**Orthogonal seminormal basis**) $\{f_t:t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)\}$ is a
   basis of $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ satisfying $f_tF_s=\delta_{ts}f_t$ and
   $\langle f_s,f_t\rangle_\lambda=\delta_{st}\langle f_t,f_t\rangle_\lambda$;
   it is the **seminormal basis** of the Murphy cell module.
4. (**Generator action**) Let $s$ be a standard $\lambda$-tableau, $1\le i<n$
   and $t:=s(i\ i+1)$, and put
   $\rho:=\operatorname{content}_s(i)-\operatorname{content}_s(i+1)\in\mathbb Z$.
   If $i$ and $i+1$ lie in the same row of $s$ then $f_sT_i=q\,f_s$; if they lie
   in the same column then $f_sT_i=-f_s$; otherwise $t$ is standard and
   $$f_sT_i=\alpha_i(s)\,f_t-\frac{1}{[\rho]_q}f_s,\qquad \alpha_i(s):=\begin{cases}1,&s\rhd t,\\[1mm]\dfrac{[1+\rho]_q[1-\rho]_q}{[\rho]_q[-\rho]_q},&t\rhd s,\end{cases}$$
   where $[-\rho]_q$ is the extended quantum integer of
   [[def-hecke-jucys-murphy-elements-and-q-contents]] and for the swapped
   tableau $\operatorname{content}_t(i)-\operatorname{content}_t(i+1)=-\rho$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^{\times}$, and $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ with
standard basis $\{T_w\}$ and star anti-automorphism $*$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]],
[[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]],
[[lem-the-star-antiautomorphism-of-the-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). For a
composition (in particular a partition) $\mu$ of $n$ put
$m_\mu:=\sum_{w\in S_\mu}T_w\in H$, the **row symmetrizer** of the standard
Young subgroup $S_\mu$
([[def-young-subgroup-tabloid-and-permutation-module]]); the sum has
$|S_\mu|=\prod_i\mu_i!$ terms.

For a row-standard $\mu$-tableau $s$
([[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]) let $d(s)\in S_n$ be the
unique permutation with $s=t^{\mu}d(s)$, where $t^{\mu}$ is the row-standard
tableau obtained by entering $1,2,\dots,n$ in increasing order from left to
right along the rows: since $t^{\mu}$ is a fixed bijection from the nodes to
$\{1,\dots,n\}$, the permutation is the row-reading word of $s$,
$d(s)(p):=s(\text{the }p\text{-th node of }[\mu]\text{ in row-major order})$.
The stabiliser of $t^\mu$ is $S_\mu$ itself, because the row sets of $t^\mu$
are exactly the blocks of $\mu$
([[def-row-and-column-stabilizers-of-a-tableau]]). For row-standard tableau
$s$ one has $d(s)\in D_\mu$, the set of distinguished right-coset
representatives of $S_\mu$: $d(s)$ is the unique element of minimal length in
the coset $S_\mu d(s)$ with respect to the inversion length
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]), and
$$\ell(wd)=\ell(w)+\ell(d)\qquad(w\in S_\mu,\ d\in D_\mu).$$
(This is the standard parabolic distinguished-representative property: since
the rows of $s$ are the blocks, $d(s)$ has no right descent $s_i$ with $i,i+1$
in the same block, and the exchange and deletion conditions of
[[lem-finite-weyl-strong-exchange-and-deletion]] upgrade this to the displayed
minimality and length additivity.)

For row-standard $\mu$-tableaux $s,t$ define the **Murphy element**
$$m_{st}:=T_{d(s)}^{*}\,m_{\mu}\,T_{d(t)}\in H,$$
and for a standard $\lambda$-tableau $t$ shorten
$m_t:=m_{tt}=T_{d(t)}^{*}m_\lambda T_{d(t)}$. Then $m_{st}^{*}=m_{ts}$ for all
row-standard $s,t$ of the same shape: applying the anti-automorphism, which
fixes $m_\mu$ because $m_\mu^*=\sum_{w\in S_\mu}T_{w^{-1}}=m_\mu$, gives
$$m_{st}^{*}=(T_{d(s)}^{*}m_\mu T_{d(t)})^{*}=T_{d(t)}^{*}m_\mu^{*}T_{d(s)}^{**}=T_{d(t)}^{*}m_\mu T_{d(s)}=m_{ts}.$$
Finally, $m_\mu T_w=q^{\ell(w)}m_\mu$ for every $w\in S_\mu$: it suffices to
prove this for $w=s_i$ a simple transposition with $i,i+1$ in the same block of
$\mu$, since any $w\in S_\mu\setminus\{1\}$ has a reduced expression
$w=w's_i$ with $\ell(w)=\ell(w')+1$ and the claim follows by induction,
$m_\mu T_w=m_\mu T_{w'}T_i=q^{\ell(w')}m_\mu T_i=q^{\ell(w)}m_\mu$. For such
$i$ the right multiplication $v\mapsto vs_i$ is an involution of the finite
group $S_\mu$, and pairing the summands of $m_\mu T_i=\sum_{v\in S_\mu}T_vT_i$
in twos gives, in the two cases of the standard-basis multiplication rule
$T_vT_i=T_{vs_i}$ if $\ell(vs_i)=\ell(v)+1$ and
$T_vT_i=(q-1)T_v+qT_{vs_i}$ if $\ell(vs_i)=\ell(v)-1$,
$$T_vT_i+T_{vs_i}T_i=q\,(T_v+T_{vs_i}),$$
so summing over the $\tfrac12|S_\mu|$ pairs yields $m_\mu T_i=qm_\mu$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^{\times}$, and $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Let $\Lambda$ be the set of partitions
of $n$ ordered by dominance $\unrhd$
([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]]), and for $\lambda\in\Lambda$ let
$T(\lambda)=\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)$ be the set of standard $\lambda$-tableaux
([[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]). Then the **Murphy basis
theorem** holds: the family
$$\mathcal M=\{m_{st}:\lambda\vdash n,\ s,t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)\}$$
is an $R$-basis of $H$, and $(\mathcal M,\Lambda)$ is a cellular basis of $H$ in
the sense of [[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]. Explicitly:
(i) $m_{st}^{*}=m_{ts}$ for all $\lambda$ and $s,t$; and (ii) for every
$\lambda$, every $t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)$ and every $h\in H$ there exist
$r_v\in R$ with
$$m_{st}h\equiv\sum_{v\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)}r_v\,m_{sv}\pmod{H^{\rhd\lambda}},$$
where $H^{\rhd\lambda}$ is spanned by the $m_{uv}$ with $\mu\rhd\lambda$. The
theorem holds over every commutative coefficient ring with $q\in R^{\times}$
and assumes no semisimplicity; the total number of Murphy elements is
$\sum_{\lambda\vdash n}|\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)|^2=n!$
([[cor-sum-of-squares-of-standard-tableau-numbers]]), matching the rank of $H$.

Let $F$ be a field, $q=1\in F$, and let $H_{F,1}(S_n)$ be the specialization of
the generic type-A Hecke algebra at $v\mapsto1$, so that
$H_{F,1}(S_n)\cong F[S_n]$ with $T_w\mapsto w$
([[prop-group-algebra-and-finite-field-specializations-of-the-generic-hecke-algebra]]).
Then the Hecke theory of this page specializes as follows.

1. The Murphy elements $m_\mu=\sum_{w\in S_\mu}T_w$ specialize to the row
   symmetrizers $\sum_{w\in S_\mu}w$, and the Murphy basis $\{m_{st}\}$ of
   $H_{F,1}(S_n)$ specializes to the Murphy basis of the group algebra
   $F[S_n]$ (the base change $\mathbb Z[S_n]\to F[S_n]$ of the integral Murphy
   basis).
2. For every $\lambda\vdash n$ the specialization of the page's Hecke Specht
   module $S^{\lambda}$ ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]) is
   the ordinary Specht module in the Dipper-James convention:
   $S^{\lambda}_{q=1}\cong S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{DJ}}$ as $F[S_n]$-modules, with
   the standard polytabloid basis ([[thm-standard-polytabloid-basis]]); the
   specialized cell form is the standard bilinear form on $S^{\lambda}$ whose
   radical defines the James quotient $D^{\lambda}$
   ([[def-modular-specht-form-and-radical-quotient]]).
3. The quantum characteristic of $q=1$ is $e=\operatorname{char}(F)$ when
   $\operatorname{char}(F)>0$, and $e=\infty$ when
   $\operatorname{char}(F)=0$
   ([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]); in
   characteristic $p>0$ a partition is $e$-regular exactly when it is
   $p$-regular. Hence $D^{\lambda}_{q=1}\ne0$ exactly for $p$-regular $\lambda$
   ([[thm-simple-type-a-hecke-modules-are-indexed-by-e-regular-partitions]]),
   and for non-$p$-regular $\lambda$ one has
   $\mathrm{rad}\,S^{\lambda}=S^{\lambda}$. This matches the group-side
   classification
   [[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]] and the
   conjugate-sign dictionary
   [[prop-p-regular-and-p-restricted-simple-labels-are-related-by-conjugate-sign-duality]].
   In characteristic $0$ the specialization is split semisimple and all Specht
   modules are irreducible.

Let $R$ be a principal ideal domain, $\pi$ a prime element, $F=R/\pi R$ the
residue field, and let $\hat q\in R^{\times}$ satisfy $[n]!_{\hat q}\ne0$ in $R$;
put $q:=\hat q+\pi R\in F^{\times}$. Let $d\ge1$, let $\lambda$ be a partition
of $n$ with at most $d$ parts, and let $W^{\lambda}_F$ be the Weyl module of the
q-Schur algebra $S_F(d,n)=S(d,n)\otimes_RF$ with its Jantzen filtration
$W^{\lambda}_F(i)$ with respect to $(R,\pi)$
([[def-jantzen-filtration-of-a-lifted-cell-module]],
[[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]).

1. (**Jantzen sum formula**) In the Grothendieck group of finite-dimensional
   $S_F(d,n)$-modules,
   $$\sum_{i>0}\bigl[W^{\lambda}_F(i)\bigr]=\sum_{\substack{(a,b),(a,c)\in[\lambda]\\ b<c}}\Bigl(\nu_\pi\bigl([h^{\lambda}_{ab}]_{\hat q}\bigr)-\nu_\pi\bigl([h^{\lambda}_{ac}]_{\hat q}\bigr)\Bigr)\Bigl[W_F^{(\beta_1,\dots,\beta_b+h^{\lambda}_{ab},\dots,\beta_c-h^{\lambda}_{ac},\dots,\beta_n)}\Bigr],$$
   where $\beta=\beta(\lambda)$ is the beta sequence of $\lambda$,
   $h^{\lambda}_{ab}$ are its hook lengths and the symbols are the virtual Weyl
   symbols of [[def-alternating-weyl-and-specht-symbols-from-beta-sequences]].
2. (**q-Schaper, $d\ge n$**) If $d\ge n$ and $\Pi$ denotes the Schur functor of
   [[def-schur-idempotent-and-schur-functor-for-type-a-q-schur-algebras]], then
   applying $\Pi$ to (1) gives the corresponding identity for the Hecke Specht
   modules in the source's normalisation, that is, for the Murphy cell modules
   $\Pi(W^{\lambda}_F)=S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ of
   [[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]] (the Dipper-James form is
   obtained by conjugating partitions and applying the same $\theta$ pullback
   to every Hecke module),
   $$\sum_{i>0}\bigl[S^{\lambda}_F(i)\bigr]=\sum_{\substack{(a,b),(a,c)\in[\lambda]\\ b<c}}\Bigl(\nu_\pi\bigl([h^{\lambda}_{ab}]_{\hat q}\bigr)-\nu_\pi\bigl([h^{\lambda}_{ac}]_{\hat q}\bigr)\Bigr)\Bigl[S_F^{(\beta_1,\dots,\beta_b+h^{\lambda}_{ab},\dots,\beta_c-h^{\lambda}_{ac},\dots,\beta_n)}\Bigr]$$
   in the Grothendieck group of finite-dimensional $H_{F,q}(S_n)$-modules, with
   the virtual Specht symbols of
   [[def-alternating-weyl-and-specht-symbols-from-beta-sequences]]. The formula
   is a virtual radical-layer identity: each nonzero coefficient bounds the
   corresponding composition multiplicity from above and forces at least one
   occurrence of the corresponding simple factor, but it is not a general
   algorithm for decomposition numbers.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $q\in R^{\times}$. With the Murphy cellular
basis $(\mathcal M,\Lambda)$ of $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$
([[thm-murphy-tableau-elements-form-a-cellular-basis]],
[[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]) and the canonical tableau
$t^\lambda$ of shape $\lambda\vdash n$
([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]]), the **Murphy cell
module** $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ is the right cell module $C^{\lambda}$ of the
Murphy basis: it is the free $R$-module with basis
$\{m_t:=m_{t^\lambda t}:t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)\}$ - the classes of the
Murphy elements whose *first* index is the canonical tableau - and $H$ acts by
$m_th=\sum_vr_vm_v$ whenever
$m_{t^\lambda t}h\equiv\sum_vr_vm_{t^\lambda v}\pmod{H^{\rhd\lambda}}$. (The
cellular action rule transforms the second index and fixes the first, so the
diagonal elements $m_{tt}$ alone do not span a submodule; the module basis is
the fixed-first-index family above.) Its **cell form** is the unique bilinear
form $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_\lambda:S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}\times
S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}\to R$ with
$$m_{us}m_{tv}\equiv\langle m_s,m_t\rangle_\lambda\,m_{uv}\pmod{H^{\rhd\lambda}}$$
for all $s,t,u,v\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)$; it is symmetric and associative and
$\mathrm{rad}\,S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ is a submodule, so
$D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}:=S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}/\mathrm{rad}\,S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$
is a right $H$-module
([[lem-cell-form-is-associative-and-its-radical-is-a-submodule]]).

**Convention (Dipper-James signed cellular normalization).** Let $\theta:H\to H$
be the involutive algebra automorphism defined by
$\theta(T_i)=-qT_i^{-1}=(q-1)-T_i$
([[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]]). For a right module $M$,
write $M^\theta$ for the same $R$-module with action $x\cdot h=x\theta(h)$. The
page's ordinary Specht normalization is the signed conjugate Murphy
construction
$$S^{\lambda}:=(S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta,$$
where $\lambda'$ is the conjugate partition ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). Its form is the form of
$S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}$ on the same underlying module; because $\theta$
commutes with $*$ this is associative for the twisted action
([[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]]). Over a field put
$$D^{\lambda}:=S^{\lambda}/\operatorname{rad}_{\rm form}S^{\lambda}=(D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta.$$
Thus $S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}=(S^{\lambda})^\theta$ and
$D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}=(D^{\lambda})^\theta$; conjugation alone does not
identify these modules
([[thm-dj-bridge-murphy-cell-is-the-same-shape-specht-dual]],
[[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]]). At
$q=1$, $\theta(\sigma)=\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\sigma$, so these identities
contain tensoring with sign; in characteristic $2$ the sign twist becomes
trivial at $q=1$
([[cor-dj-bridge-specialization-and-composition-multiplicity-dictionary]]).
The nonzero quotients in this signed normalization have $e$-regular labels
because the nonzero Murphy quotients have conjugate $e$-restricted labels
([[def-e-regular-and-e-restricted-partitions]]). No generic root-of-unity
Hecke claim is inferred from the published prime-characteristic group-only sign
dictionary, and no semisimplicity or choice principle is assumed.

Let $F$ be a field, $q\in F^{\times}$, $e=e(F,q)$ and $H=H_{F,q}(S_n)$
([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]). For
$\lambda\vdash n$ and $e$-regular $\mu\vdash n$ let
$$d_{\lambda\mu}:=[S^{\lambda}:D^{\mu}],$$
the multiplicity of $D^{\mu}$ in a composition series of the Specht module
$S^{\lambda}$ ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]],
[[thm-simple-type-a-hecke-modules-are-indexed-by-e-regular-partitions]]). Then
$$d_{\mu\mu}=1\qquad\text{and}\qquad d_{\lambda\mu}\ne0\ \Longrightarrow\ \mu\unrhd\lambda,$$
where $\unrhd$ is the dominance order on partitions
([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]]): a simple factor $D^{\mu}$ of
$S^{\lambda}$ can occur only if the $e$-regular label $\mu$ dominates
$\lambda$. Equivalently the decomposition matrix $(d_{\lambda\mu})$ is
unitriangular along dominance. This constrains but does not compute the
entries: no off-diagonal decomposition number is determined by cellularity.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$ and $A$ a unital $R$-algebra
([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) that is free as an $R$-module on a
finite set $C=\{c^{\lambda}_{st}:\lambda\in\Lambda,\ s,t\in T(\lambda)\}$,
where $(\Lambda,\unrhd)$ is a finite poset ([[def-partial-order]]; its strict
order is written $\rhd$) and each $T(\lambda)$ is a finite set. For
$\lambda\in\Lambda$ let $A^{\rhd\lambda}$ be the $R$-submodule of $A$ spanned
by all $c^{\mu}_{uv}$ with $\mu\rhd\lambda$.

Then $(C,\Lambda)$ is a **cellular basis** of $A$, and $A$ is a **cellular
algebra**, if:

(i) the $R$-linear map $i:A\to A$ with $i(c^{\lambda}_{st})=c^{\lambda}_{ts}$
for all $\lambda,s,t$ is an algebra anti-automorphism of $A$, i.e. $i(ab)=i(b)i(a)$
and $i(1)=1$ (equivalently $i$ is an isomorphism of $A$ with the opposite
algebra; the displayed formula forces $i^2=\mathrm{id}$); and

(ii) for every $\lambda\in\Lambda$, every $t\in T(\lambda)$ and every $a\in A$
there exist $r_v\in R$ ($v\in T(\lambda)$) with
$$c^{\lambda}_{st}\,a\equiv\sum_{v\in T(\lambda)}r_v\,c^{\lambda}_{sv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}.$$

**Cell modules.** For $\lambda\in\Lambda$ let $C^{\lambda}$ be the free
$R$-module with basis $\{c^{\lambda}_t:=c^{\lambda}_{tt}:t\in T(\lambda)\}$;
condition (ii) makes $C^{\lambda}$ a right $A$-module by
$c^{\lambda}_t a:=\sum_v r_vc^{\lambda}_v$ when
$c^{\lambda}_{tt}a\equiv\sum_v r_vc^{\lambda}_{tv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}$, and
it makes $C^{\lambda}$ a left $A$-module via $i$, the left action being
$a\cdot c^{\lambda}_t:=c^{\lambda}_t\,i(a)$. Both actions are well defined on
the freely spanning basis elements by (ii): the coefficients $r_v$ are unique
because $C$ is an $R$-basis of $A$ and the quotient by $A^{\rhd\lambda}$ kills
exactly the basis elements indexed by strictly larger labels, while applying
the anti-automorphism (i) to (ii) gives the same triangularity for left
multiplication. The module $C^{\lambda}$ is the **(right) cell module** of
$\lambda$, and
$$A^{\unrhd\lambda}/A^{\rhd\lambda}\cong C^{\lambda}\otimes_R C^{\lambda}$$
via $c^{\lambda}_{st}+A^{\rhd\lambda}\mapsto c^{\lambda}_s\otimes c^{\lambda}_t$,
where $A^{\unrhd\lambda}$ is spanned by all $c^{\mu}_{uv}$ with
$\mu\unrhd\lambda$. A cellular algebra may have several cellular bases.

Let $F$ be a field and $A$ a finite-dimensional unital cellular $F$-algebra with
cellular basis $(C,\Lambda)$ over the finite poset $\Lambda$
([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]). For $\lambda\in\Lambda$
put $D^{\lambda}:=C^{\lambda}/\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$, where
$\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$ is the radical of the cell form
([[lem-cell-form-is-associative-and-its-radical-is-a-submodule]]). Then:

1. if $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ then $D^{\lambda}$ is an absolutely irreducible
   (absolutely simple) $A$-module: it is simple over $F$ and remains simple
   after every extension of scalars to a larger field;
2. $\{D^{\lambda}:\lambda\in\Lambda,\ D^{\lambda}\ne0\}$ is a complete set of
   pairwise non-isomorphic simple $A$-modules ([[def-simple-module]],
   [[thm-jordan-holder-theorem-for-modules]]);
3. $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ if and only if the cell form
   $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_\lambda$ is not identically zero, if and only if
   $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}\ne C^{\lambda}$; and, when these equivalent
   conditions hold, $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$ is the unique maximal proper
   submodule and the Jacobson radical of $C^{\lambda}$, so $D^{\lambda}$ is its
   simple head. If the form is identically zero, the cell-form quotient
   $D^{\lambda}$ is zero; no assertion about the Jacobson radical or the actual
   head of $C^{\lambda}$ is made.

No semisimplicity of $A$ is assumed; the theorem is the Graham-Lehrer
classification and applies in particular to $A=H_{F,q}(S_n)$ for every field
$F$ and every $q\in F^{\times}$.

Let $e\in\{2,3,4,\dots\}\cup\{\infty\}$ and let $\lambda\vdash n$ be a partition
with parts $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots$ and conjugate $\lambda'$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). Then $\lambda$ is
**$e$-regular** when every positive integer occurs as a part of $\lambda$ fewer
than $e$ times, i.e. $z_j(\lambda)<e$ for every $j\ge1$, and **$e$-restricted**
when $\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}<e$ for every $i\ge1$ (with $\lambda_i:=0$ for
$i>\ell(\lambda)$).

For finite $e$ these are exactly the $p$-regular and $p$-restricted notions of
[[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]] with $p=e$. For $e=\infty$ both
conditions are vacuous, so every partition is both $e$-regular and
$e$-restricted: the inequalities $z_j(\lambda)<\infty$ and
$\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}<\infty$ hold because partitions have finitely many
nonzero parts and each difference is a nonnegative integer. Moreover $\lambda$
is $e$-restricted if and only if its conjugate $\lambda'$ is $e$-regular: the
multiplicity of the part $i$ in $\lambda'$ is the number of columns of
$[\lambda]$ of height exactly $i$, namely $\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}$, so the
two conditions $z_i(\lambda')=\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}<e$ are the same family
of inequalities, and for $e=\infty$ both sides hold. In particular
$\varnothing$ is simultaneously $e$-regular and $e$-restricted for every $e$
([[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]]).

Let $F$ be a field, $q\in F^{\times}$, let
$e=e(F,q)\in\{2,3,\dots\}\cup\{\infty\}$ be the quantum characteristic
([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]) and let
$H=H_{F,q}(S_n)$ for $n\ge0$. For $\lambda\vdash n$ let $S^{\lambda}$ be the
Hecke Specht module and $D^{\lambda}=S^{\lambda}/\mathrm{rad}\,S^{\lambda}$ its
cell-form quotient ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]). Then:

1. $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ if and only if $\lambda$ is $e$-regular
   ([[def-e-regular-and-e-restricted-partitions]]);
2. $\{D^{\lambda}:\lambda\vdash n\text{ is }e\text{-regular}\}$ is a complete
   set of pairwise non-isomorphic absolutely irreducible $H$-modules;
3. $H$ is split semisimple if and only if $e>n$ (including $e=\infty$); when
   $e\le n$ the algebra has nonzero radical.

This is the exact root-of-unity replacement for the ordinary Specht
classification. At $q=1$ in characteristic $p>0$ it specialises to the
classification of the simple $F[S_n]$-modules by $p$-regular partitions
([[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]]). No
semisimplicity is assumed and no choice principle is used.

Let $R$ be a principal ideal domain, $\pi$ a prime element, $F=R/\pi R$ the
residue field, and let $\hat q\in R^{\times}$ satisfy $[n]!_{\hat q}\ne0$ in $R$;
put $q:=\hat q+\pi R\in F^{\times}$. Let $d\ge1$, let $\lambda$ be a partition
of $n$ with at most $d$ parts, and let $W^{\lambda}_F$ be the Weyl module of the
q-Schur algebra $S_F(d,n)=S(d,n)\otimes_RF$ with its Jantzen filtration
$W^{\lambda}_F(i)$ with respect to $(R,\pi)$
([[def-jantzen-filtration-of-a-lifted-cell-module]],
[[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]).

1. (**Jantzen sum formula**) In the Grothendieck group of finite-dimensional
   $S_F(d,n)$-modules,
   $$\sum_{i>0}\bigl[W^{\lambda}_F(i)\bigr]=\sum_{\substack{(a,b),(a,c)\in[\lambda]\\ b<c}}\Bigl(\nu_\pi\bigl([h^{\lambda}_{ab}]_{\hat q}\bigr)-\nu_\pi\bigl([h^{\lambda}_{ac}]_{\hat q}\bigr)\Bigr)\Bigl[W_F^{(\beta_1,\dots,\beta_b+h^{\lambda}_{ab},\dots,\beta_c-h^{\lambda}_{ac},\dots,\beta_n)}\Bigr],$$
   where $\beta=\beta(\lambda)$ is the beta sequence of $\lambda$,
   $h^{\lambda}_{ab}$ are its hook lengths and the symbols are the virtual Weyl
   symbols of [[def-alternating-weyl-and-specht-symbols-from-beta-sequences]].
2. (**q-Schaper, $d\ge n$**) If $d\ge n$ and $\Pi$ denotes the Schur functor of
   [[def-schur-idempotent-and-schur-functor-for-type-a-q-schur-algebras]], then
   applying $\Pi$ to (1) gives the corresponding identity for the Hecke Specht
   modules in the source's normalisation, that is, for the Murphy cell modules
   $\Pi(W^{\lambda}_F)=S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ of
   [[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]] (the Dipper-James form is
   obtained by conjugating partitions and applying the same $\theta$ pullback
   to every Hecke module),
   $$\sum_{i>0}\bigl[S^{\lambda}_F(i)\bigr]=\sum_{\substack{(a,b),(a,c)\in[\lambda]\\ b<c}}\Bigl(\nu_\pi\bigl([h^{\lambda}_{ab}]_{\hat q}\bigr)-\nu_\pi\bigl([h^{\lambda}_{ac}]_{\hat q}\bigr)\Bigr)\Bigl[S_F^{(\beta_1,\dots,\beta_b+h^{\lambda}_{ab},\dots,\beta_c-h^{\lambda}_{ac},\dots,\beta_n)}\Bigr]$$
   in the Grothendieck group of finite-dimensional $H_{F,q}(S_n)$-modules, with
   the virtual Specht symbols of
   [[def-alternating-weyl-and-specht-symbols-from-beta-sequences]]. The formula
   is a virtual radical-layer identity: each nonzero coefficient bounds the
   corresponding composition multiplicity from above and forces at least one
   occurrence of the corresponding simple factor, but it is not a general
   algorithm for decomposition numbers.

Take $R=\mathbb C[\hat q]$, the prime element $\pi=1+\hat q$ (so that
$F=\mathbb C$ and $q:=\hat q+\pi R$ specialises to $-1$, giving $e=2$), and
$\lambda=(3,2)$, $n=5$. Evaluating the q-Schaper virtual sums
([[thm-q-schaper-virtual-radical-layer-formula]]) with the hook valuations
$\nu_\pi([2]_{\hat q})=\nu_\pi([4]_{\hat q})=1$,
$\nu_\pi([3]_{\hat q})=\nu_\pi([1]_{\hat q})=0$ gives, in the source's
normalisation,
$$\sum_{i>0}\bigl[W^{(3,2)}_F(i)\bigr]=\bigl[W^{(3,1^2)}_F\bigr]+\bigl[W^{(2^2,1)}_F\bigr]-\bigl[W^{(1^5)}_F\bigr],\qquad \sum_{i>0}\bigl[S^{(3,2)}_F(i)\bigr]=2\bigl[D^{(2^2,1)}_{\mathrm{M}}\bigr].$$
Further Jantzen calculations give $W^{(1^5)}_F=L^{(1^5)}_F$,
$W^{(2^2,1)}_F=L^{(2^2,1)}_F$ and
$W^{(3,1^2)}_F\sim L^{(3,1^2)}_F+L^{(2^2,1)}_F+L^{(1^5)}_F$, so at the level of
the sum formula alone one gets $d_{(3,2),(3,1^2)}=1$ and only the bound
$d_{(3,2),(2^2,1)}\in\{1,2\}$. The extra dimension/filtration argument on the
Specht side gives
$S^{(3,2)}_{\mathrm{M}}\cong D^{(2^2,1)}_{\mathrm{M}}$ (both sides have
dimension $5$), whence $d_{(3,2),(2^2,1)}=1$: the virtual sum alone did not
determine the entry. Translated to the Dipper-James convention of this page by
conjugating and applying the same $\theta$ pullback to both modules
([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]), this reads
$S^{(2,2,1)}_{\mathrm{DJ}}\cong D^{(3,2)}_{\mathrm{DJ}}$, while the partition
$(2,2,1)$ is not $2$-regular, so its own labelled head vanishes,
$D^{(2,2,1)}_{\mathrm{DJ}}=0$. The computed entry is consistent with the
dominance bound $d_{\lambda\mu}\ne0\Rightarrow\mu\unrhd\lambda$ of
[[cor-type-a-hecke-decomposition-matrix-is-dominance-unitriangular]].

derivations.claim: The abstract instance: in $A=F[x]/(x^2)$ with $c_{11}=1$, $c_{22}=x$ and $2\rhd1$, the product $c_{22}c_{22}=x^2=0$ is congruent to $0\cdot c_{22}$ modulo $A^{\rhd2}=0$, so the axiom holds with zero form value; the products $c_{11}(a+bx)=a+bx\equiv a\,c_{11}\pmod{(x)}$ and $c_{22}(a+bx)=ax=a\,c_{22}$ confirm the triangularity. Hence $C^{2}$ has identically zero form, $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{2}=C^{2}$ and $D^{2}=0$; the module $C^{2}$ itself is one-dimensional with $a+bx$ acting as $a$, hence simple with zero Jacobson radical and head $C^{2}\ne0$. Moreover $x\in A$ is a nonzero nilpotent, so $\mathrm{rad}\,A=(x)\ne0$ and $A$ is not semisimple.

The Hecke instance: for $F$ of characteristic $2$ and $q=1$ the sign module is the trivial module, so the Murphy cell module $S^{(3)}_{\mathrm M}$ and its theta-pullback $S^{(1,1,1)}=(S^{(3)}_{\mathrm M})^\theta$ are the trivial module; the label $(1,1,1)$ is not $2$-regular, so by [F2] $D^{(1,1,1)}=0$ while $S^{(1,1,1)}\ne0$.

The reducible Weyl module: by [F3] the sum of the positive Jantzen layers of $W^{(3,2)}_F$ is a nonzero virtual class; since the total dimension of the positive layers equals the valuation of the Gram determinant, the radical $\mathrm{rad}\,W^{(3,2)}_F=F\otimes\mathrm{rad}$ is nonzero and $W^{(3,2)}_F$ is reducible, although its head $L^{(3,2)}_F$ is simple.

Conclusion: the three instances refute the claims that cellularity forces semisimplicity, forces every cell module to be simple, or forces every labelled cell-form quotient to be nonzero; each is an application of the classification of cell-form quotients [F1] together with the explicit degenerate data.

boundaries.evidence: The Statement refuted asserts that a labelled quotient may vanish; in the abstract instance the cell C^2=(x) is nonzero while its cell-form quotient D^2 is zero, so the empty case D^lambda=0 is exhibited rather than excluded.
